CS 6672 · hacker presentation

GhostMap

Cornell, rebuilt from internet photographs inside the world's own 3D model.

Geographically grounded · Time-aware · Visually immersive

Where. COLMAP fragments placed in metres on public lidar, with no GPS, and a certificate that says when the evidence is not enough.
How it looked. Gaussian splats from the same photographs, judged by the lidar and taught by it.
When. Twenty years of aerial flights, documented dates and dated photographs in one frame.

Public data only: USGS 3DEP lidar, New York State orthoimagery, OpenStreetMap, Wikimedia Commons and Flickr (via Openverse) under their licences. No annotation, no geotags, no hand-picked correspondences.

Open with the one-line idea: the US already has a public 3D model of itself (lidar). Internet-photo reconstructions have always lived in a vacuum. We put them inside it — and then use it as a referee and a teacher.
The idea

The world already has a 3D model. Internet reconstructions ignore it.

  • USGS 3DEP airborne lidar covers most of the United States, public domain: roofs, ground and trees in metres.
  • COLMAP on internet photographs gives a fragment in its own frame: unknown scale, unknown up, unknown north.
  • GPS would fix that, but most photographs carry none.
  • So we ask three questions inside one metric frame: where is the fragment, how did the place look, when did it change?
The lidar is not just a backdrop: it places the reconstruction, scores it, and trains it.
The Arts Quad and the Gates Hall site: 2020 lidar terrain draped with the New York State aerial flight of the selected year.
Numbers on this slide come from the data: how many photographs, how many have GPS, how many of those are plausible.
Why this is a COLMAP hack

Where COLMAP stops, and what we built past it

COLMAP on internet photographsGhostMap addsMeasured here
1A model in its own frame: no scale, no north, no up. A map needs GPS or hand-picked control points.Placement without GPS, inside public lidar and building footprints—
2Never says when a placement cannot be trusted.A certificate: which cue fixed what, or a refusal with the reason—
3Disconnected fragments, each in its own frame.One shared world frame—
4Splats trained on its output float paint in mid-air, unchecked.The lidar as referee and as teacher—
5One static scene: twenty years blended into one moment.Years per point; dated buildings and aerial flights—
6Registers a new photograph only into that same frame of its own.A new photograph placed on the campus in seconds, with a certificate, painted back onto the lidar city—
The hack in one line: COLMAP's frame is arbitrary, so search for the one similarity transform that puts the reconstruction inside the world's own 3D model, and say when no such transform is determined.
This is the slide that answers "why is this a COLMAP project". Everything starts from COLMAP's cameras and points; each row is a limit we hit on real internet photographs and the chapter of the demo that shows our answer. Live demo chapter 0 has the same six cards with links.

Where · 2

Snap to the world, without GPS

One similarity (scale, rotation, translation) from cues the public data can check:

  • Gravity from facade normals (walls are vertical).
  • Walls: points on OpenStreetMap footprint walls, precision and recall, so nothing shrinks onto one wall line.
  • Roof edges: the facade top meets the lidar roof edge of its wall.
  • Camera height: photographers stand at eye height on the lidar ground.
  • Landmark: a tower's axis on its footprint, its top at the lidar top.
  • Free space: no ray from a camera to its points passes through a building.
The certificate says which cue fixed the scale.
Live demo, chapter 2: the snap animation and the certificate.
Stress: no geotags, no manual correspondences. The landmark method reproduced: same placement within about a percent in scale and a degree in rotation.
Where · 3

A certificate, not just an answer

The fit's objective over scale (the best yaw and position at each scale), all cues and each cue alone. A peaked curve means the scale is determined; a flat one means it is not.

Cue ablation: refit from the optimum with one cue removed; how far scale, yaw and position move.

The yaw of a square tower is ambiguous by 90 degrees; here the library walls break the symmetry: the other quadrants score far below the best.
Where · 4

Knowing when it can't

Every fragment of the campus-wide run with eight or more photographs, refused for a stated reason:

No fragment was certified and then found wrong.

Synthetic hall with a known answer: what the facades in view can fix.

Exact lidar roof edges, all cues. One facade cannot fix its own scale; two parallel facades cannot fix where along them the fragment sits.

This is the failure taxonomy: no facade seen (close-ups), scale undetermined (one facade), yaw ambiguous (a square tower), cues disagree, cameras inside buildings.

The lidar as referee

A Gaussian splat trained from the same photographs, in the lidar frame. Every Gaussian is judged against the lidar:

—on lidar surfaces

Per building: …

The fragment's own sparse points set the noise floor.

The first in-the-wild reconstruction score anyone can reproduce wherever 3DEP lidar exists.

A photograph the splat never saw (left) and the plain splat rendered at its pose by gsplat (right), colour fitted to the photograph. In the live demo, chapter 4 colours every Gaussian by the lidar's verdict.
Floaters are the classic failure of in-the-wild splats; for the first time we can count them against a measurement instead of eyeballing renders.
How it looked · 2

The lidar as teacher

Same photographs, same steps; one extra term: the lidar's measured free space is empty. Gaussians in it fade, and those far in the air are removed.

The floaters disappear.

A view between the photographers that nobody took, every Gaussian painted by the lidar's verdict (red: in air the lidar measured empty): plain splat (left), lidar-taught (right), rendered by gsplat.
At a held-out photograph's pose: plain (left), lidar-taught (right).
In chapter 5 of the demo, the fly-through: both splats side by side, the map (lower left) shows the camera among the photographers, and at each photographer's spot the real photograph appears. Then tick "paint each Gaussian by the lidar's verdict": red is paint in air the lidar measured empty, purple is under the bare ground.
When · 1

Twenty years in one frame

  • From above: six public aerial flights (2002–2023) on the 2020 lidar terrain; buildings flattened before their documented construction.
  • Gates Hall: a parking lot until 2012; site works in 2012; finished roof from the 2015 flight.
  • Klarman Hall: the courtyard behind Goldwin Smith Hall until 2012; under construction in 2015.
  • McGraw Tower: every point carries the years photographs saw it (2003–2025).

Documented dates decide when a building appears; the aerial edge score is shown as a diagnostic, never as the decision.

Live demo, chapters 6 to 9: the year slider.
Honesty

What the record cannot show

  • No licensed ground-level photograph of any site before construction exists online: the "before" is aerial only.
  • One facade cannot fix its own scale, and close-ups of an entrance see no facade at all: those fragments are refused, not placed.
  • Airborne lidar sees roofs and ground densely, walls thinly: distances on walls are conservative; the free-space test uses a 2.5 m horizontal tolerance.
  • Splats keep what the photographs saw: the far side of the tower and roofs nobody photographed stay empty.
  • Boardman Hall (demolished 1959): its postcards register only as mirror images; no licensed modern photograph looks from the side they were taken.
A new photograph

A photograph it has never seen

Drop a photograph of the tower: the most similar of the fragment's photographs are found, matched, and RANSAC says where the photographer stood and which way they looked, in seconds and without GPS. COLMAP could only register it into its own frame.

Then it is painted back onto the lidar city from that pose. If the placement is right, its walls land on the lidar's walls.

Placed, or refused with the reason.

A long lens on a distant tower fixes the direction but not the distance: then the certificate says so, and the page draws where along the line of sight the photographer may have stood instead of painting from the wrong place.

Live demo, chapter 11.
Drop one of your own phone photographs of the tower (from Ho Plaza or Libe Slope) onto chapter 11, or pick one from the tray. Click "stand where the photographer stood", then drag the slider from photograph to city: the silhouettes stay put. End with "paint the photographs back".

Reproducible

Public data in, every number traceable out

  • Stages under pipeline/ghostmap/: acquire → prepare → sfm → anchor → dense/splats → evaluate → web; each writes a JSON report the page and these slides read.
  • COLMAP (pycolmap), SuperPoint + LightGlue, NetVLAD; gsplat; on one laptop GPU (RTX 3070 Ti), the CUDA compiler installed without root.
  • Unit tests for every estimator piece, synthetic halls with known answers, browser checks of every chapter.
